Scatterplot showing the relationship between chemical concentration and reproductive output in C. elegans.* 5.0.3 Scatterplot normalized data neg_mean <- C.elegans %>% filter(expType == "controlNegative") %>% summarise(mean_val = mean(RawData, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_val) C.elegans_normalized <- C.elegans %>% mutate(normData = RawData / neg_mean) ggplot(C.elegans_normalized, aes( x = compConcentration, y = normData, color = compName, shape = expType )) + geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.05), na.rm = TRUE) + scale_x_log10() + theme_minimal() + labs(title = "Effect of chemical concentration on C. elegans reproduction", x = "Concentration (nM, log10 scale)", y = "Relative offspring count (normalized to negative control)") ## Warning in scale_x_log10(): log-10 transformation introduced infinite values. Figure 2. Scatterplot showing the relationship between chemical concentration and reproductive output in C. elegans, with normalized data.* 5.0.4 Analyse 5.0.4.1 Controls The negative control is the condition in which C. elegans is not exposed to any chemical. This represents the baseline condition and serves as a reference value for the experiment. The positive control is a condition in which C. elegans is exposed to a chemical with a known effect on reproduction, in this case ethanol. This control is used to verify that the experimental setup is functioning correctly and is capable of detecting an effect. The vehicle control is a condition in which only the solvent (vehicle) is present, without any active chemical. This control is used to determine whether the solvent itself has any effect on the reproduction of C. elegans. 5.0.4.2 Normalization The data were normalized to the negative control by dividing each observation by the mean value of the negative control group. As a result, the average response of the negative control is set to 1, and all other values are expressed as a fraction of this baseline. This normalization reduces variability between measurements and allows for a more direct comparison between treatments. It ensures that observed effects are interpreted relative to normal biological conditions rather than absolute counts. 5.0.5 Dose–response analysis The dose–response curve is used to estimate the IC50 value, defined as the concentration that reduces reproductive output by 50% relative to the control condition. For IC50 estimation, each chemical is analysed separately. To construct the dose–response curve, the response variable is normalized and the concentration variable is ensured to be numeric. Dose–response modelling is performed in R using the drc package. Several models are available; however, the four-parameter log-logistic model is commonly applied due to its suitability for sigmoidal dose–response relationships. Following model fitting, the IC50 is derived using the ED() function, which calculates the effective dose corresponding to a predefined response level, in this case 50%. Finally, IC50 values across different chemicals can be compared to assess relative toxicity. Lower IC50 values indicate higher potency, reflecting a stronger inhibitory effect on the reproductive output of C. elegans. 5.1 Article evaluation 5.1.0.1 Reference Geeleher P, Cox N, Huang RS (2014) pRRophetic: An R Package for Prediction of Clinical Chemotherapeutic Response from Tumor Gene Expression Levels. PLoS ONE 9(9): e107468. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0107468 5.1.0.2 Research question The aim of the study is to develop an R package that predicts chemotherapeutic response using gene expression data. 5.1.0.3 Methods Gene expression data from cancer cell lines are used as training data. The data are normalized and filtered to remove low-variation genes. The model is trained using gene expression data from cancer cell lines together with drug sensitivity (IC50) values. This model is applied to tumor gene expression data to estimate drug response in patients. 5.1.0.4 Results The package can successfully predict chemotherapy response in multiple datasets. For example, it can distinguish between responders and non-responders in multiple patients treated with bortezomib. Predictions also correlate well with measured drug sensitivity in independent cell line datasets. Using biological context (e.g., specific cancer types) improves prediction accuracy. 5.1.1 Reproducibility of the Article The article has a clearly stated study purpose, which can be found in the introduction and abstract. The goal of the study is to develop an R package (pRRophetic) that can predict chemotherapy response using gene expression data. The article also includes a data availability statement that explains that all data are publicly available without restrictions. The data and code can be accessed through the project website, and a GitHub repository. The authors are from universities and include a contact email. There is no explicit ethics statement in the article. This is likely because the study uses existing cancer cell line data and public datasets, so no human participants were directly involved. The article also includes a funding statement that shows the research was supported by several grants. Finally, the code used in the study is available as an R package and on GitHub, which makes it possible to reproduce the analysis. ### Reproducibility of the code 5.1.1.1 What can the code do? The R code takes gene expression data from cancer samples and uses it to predict how sensitive a tumor is to chemotherapy drugs. First, the data is cleaned and normalized. Then a statistical model (ridge regression) is trained using cancer cell line data where drug response is already known. After that, the model is used to predict drug sensitivity in new tumor samples. The code is simple and the structure is good. Code readability score: 4/5 5.1.1.2 Reproducibility The original pRRophetic repository is no longer actively maintained and is marked as legacy. The latest version of the package is pRRophetic2, available via OSF. Because of this, the original GitHub installation did not work, which limited full reproducibility of the original analysis. Figure 1 from the paper could not be fully reproduced due to lack of direct access to the original datasets and dependency issues in the pRRophetic pipeline. Therefore, a simplified reproduction was created to demonstrate the same analytical concept: (1) comparison between responders and non-responders, and (2) correlation between predicted and measured drug response. Overall, the reproducibility is limited, but the main analytical idea can still be recreated in a simplified form. Reproducibility score: 3/5

6 SQL 6.1 Introduction In this assignment, I worked with SQL and PostgreSQL to manipulate and combine multiple datasets. The datasets contained information about flu cases, dengue cases, and demographic information from the Gapminder dataset. The goal was to clean the datasets, import them into PostgreSQL, perform joins using SQL queries, and visualize the resulting data in R. 6.2 Preperation The flu and dengue datasets were originally in wide format. I used pivot_longer() to convert them into tidy datasets where each row represented one country at one date. Missing values were removed using filter(!is.na(cases)). A year variable was extracted from the date column using the lubridate package. Before importing the data into PostgreSQL, I converted the variables to consistent data types such as numeric, integer, character, and date. 6.3 Dbeaver I created a PostgreSQL database called workflowsdb in DBeaver. The cleaned CSV files were imported as separate tables. SQL queries were used to inspect the data and verify that the variables were imported correctly. 6.4 SQL join I used SQL LEFT JOIN statements to combine the flu, dengue, and gapminder tables. The datasets were joined on the variables country and year. A LEFT JOIN was used to ensure that all flu observations remained in the final dataset, even if information from the other datasets was missing. 6.5 Visualisaties After exporting the merged dataset from PostgreSQL, I imported it into R for visualization. Scatterplots were created to explore relationships between flu cases, dengue cases, and demographic variables such as life expectancy and GDP. This graph shows the relationship between flu cases and dengue cases. Each point represents a country in a specific year. The plot shows that flu cases vary widely, while dengue cases are generally lower. This graph shows the relationship between GDP and life expectancy. In general, countries with a higher GDP tend to have a higher life expectancy. However, there is still variation between countries.

8 Introduction to the project Prostate cancer is one of the most common types of cancer among men worldwide [@wcrf2024prostate]. Treatment options for prostate cancer include surgery, radiotherapy, hormone therapy, and systemic treatments such as chemotherapy or immunotherapy in advanced stages [@eau2023prostate]. Decision-making in prostate cancer care can be supported by a patients-like-me dashboard that shows outcomes and experiences of similar patients, helping patients and clinicians make more informed decisions [@umcu2026dashboard]. For this project, a data-driven dashboard is developed to support shared decision-making in prostate cancer care. The dashboard provides clinicians and patients with an overview of treatment options and the effects of different treatments on patient-reported outcomes, including EPIC-26 and IPSS scores. EPIC-26 (Expanded Prostate Cancer Index Composite – 26 item version) is a validated questionnaire that measures health-related quality of life in prostate cancer patients. It assesses urinary, bowel, sexual, and hormonal function domains and is widely used to evaluate treatment-related side effects [@umich_epic2024]. IPSS (International Prostate Symptom Score) is a standardized clinical questionnaire used to assess the severity of urinary symptoms and monitor changes over time [@resref_ipss2024]. Together, these measures provide important insight into both functional outcomes and quality of life after different treatment options.

9 COVID-19 Data Analysis Report (Europe) This report analyzes COVID-19 cases and deaths using a parameterized R Markdown workflow. ## Parameters For this assignment, a parameterized R Markdown report was developed to analyze COVID-19 data for European countries. The report uses three parameters: * Country * Year * Months By changing these parameters, the report automatically updates the dataset and regenerates the analysis without modifying the code. The data is retrieved from an open COVID-19 dataset provided by the ECDC. The dataset is then filtered based on the selected parameters to ensure that only relevant observations are included in the analysis. At the top of the report, the selected parameters are displayed to make the input values transparent. The report generates two visualizations: A time series plot of daily COVID-19 cases A time series plot of COVID-19 related deaths These graphs clearly show the development of COVID-19 over time for the selected country and time period. 10 Learning a new skill The skill that is learned is ‘Learning to apply machine learning techniques to predict whether a person has cancer or not’. Machine learning is becoming important in bioinformatics and medical data analysis. In biomedical research and diagnostics, machine learning models are often used to recognize patterns in large datasets and make predictions about diseases such as cancer. This skill aligns with future plans within bioinformatics because it combines programming, statistics, and biological data analysis. I learned about machine learning concepts from two YouTube videos [@video1] and [@video2]. These videos helped me understand the main types of machine learning and how they differ from each other. The first video focused on explaining supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning in a general way. The second video gave practical examples of how machine learning models learn patterns from data and use these patterns to make predictions. 10.2.1 Key concepts learned: Supervised learning Supervised learning is a type of machine learning where the model is trained using labeled data. This means that both the input data and the correct output are known. In this project, cancer prediction is an example of supervised learning because the model learns from labeled medical data (cancer vs. no cancer). Unsupervised learning Unsupervised learning is when the model works with data that has no labels. The goal is to find patterns or structures in the data without predefined answers. Reinforcement learning Reinforcement learning is a method where an agent learns by interacting with an environment and receiving rewards or penalties based on its actions. 10.2.2 Conclusion After watching both videos, I now understand the basic differences between the main types of machine learning and how supervised learning is especially relevant for cancer prediction tasks. 10.2.3 Step 2 — Learning R tools In this step, tutorials were followed to learn how to use machine learning packages in RStudio. The focus was on learning how to load packages, work with data, and train basic machine learning models. I also followed a YouTube tutorial focused on the caret package for machine learning in R. This video explained how to use caret to build machine learning models, including how to split data into training and test sets, train models, and evaluate their performance. This tutorial helped me understand the basic workflow of machine learning in RStudio. I learned how the caret package can be used to split datasets, train models, and evaluate predictions. The target variable is Class, and all other variables are used as predictors. model <- train(Class ~ ., data = training, method = "rf") model ## Random Forest ## ## 513 samples ## 9 predictor ## 2 classes: 'benign', 'malignant' ## ## No pre-processing ## Resampling: Bootstrapped (25 reps) ## Summary of sample sizes: 513, 513, 513, 513, 513, 513, ... ## Resampling results across tuning parameters: ## ## mtry Accuracy Kappa ## 2 0.9722993 0.9389574 ## 5 0.9676615 0.9284982 ## 9 0.9617083 0.9152379 ## ## Accuracy was used to select the optimal model using the largest value. ## The final value used for the model was mtry = 2. 10.7 Step 6 — Model evaluation The confusion matrix made it easier to understand how well the model predicted the correct cancer classes. predictions <- predict(model, testing) confusionMatrix(predictions, testing$Class) ## Confusion Matrix and Statistics ## ## Reference ## Prediction benign malignant ## benign 107 0 ## malignant 4 59 ## ## Accuracy : 0.9765 ## 95% CI : (0.9409, 0.9936) ## No Information Rate : 0.6529 ## P-Value [Acc > NIR] : <2e-16 ## ## Kappa : 0.9489 ## ## Mcnemar's Test P-Value : 0.1336 ## ## Sensitivity : 0.9640 ## Specificity : 1.0000 ## Pos Pred Value : 1.0000 ## Neg Pred Value : 0.9365 ## Prevalence : 0.6529 ## Detection Rate : 0.6294 ## Detection Prevalence : 0.6294 ## Balanced Accuracy : 0.9820 ## ## 'Positive' Class : benign ## 10.8 Final conclusion In this project, machine learning techniques were applied to predict cancer classes using the Breast Cancer Wisconsin dataset. During the project, important machine learning steps were learned, including data exploration, preprocessing, model training, and model evaluation. A Random Forest model was trained and evaluated using a training and test dataset. The results showed that machine learning can successfully classify cancer-related data with high accuracy. This project improved understanding of machine learning workflows in RStudio and demonstrated how machine learning can be applied in bioinformatics and biomedical research.
